title: Reverse Linked List
summary: Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head.
statement:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return the new head.

Lists are written as arrays in the tests, so `[1,2,3]` is `1 → 2 → 3`, and `[]` is an empty list (`head` is `null`).
hints: Walk the list once and point each node back at the node before it.
Keep three references: prev (starts null), curr, and next (saved before you overwrite curr.next).
Loop: next = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next. At the end prev is the new head. A recursive version is a good second exercise.
explain: Each `next` pointer is turned around, so the last node becomes the head and the list reads `[5,4,3,2,1]`.

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
summary: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list by splicing their nodes together; return its head.
statement:
`list1` and `list2` are sorted in non-decreasing order. Merge them into one sorted list by splicing together the existing nodes (no new value nodes), and return its head.

Either list may be empty.

When the front values are equal, either node can go first. Once one list runs out, attach the rest of the other in one step.
constraints: Both lists are sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: At every step the next node of the result is the smaller of the two current heads.
A dummy head node avoids special-casing the first node: keep a tail pointer and attach the smaller node to tail.next.
When one list runs out, attach the rest of the other list in one step.
explain: Repeatedly take the smaller front node of the two lists: 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 4. The merged list is `[1,1,2,3,4,4]`.

title: Remove Linked List Elements
summary: Remove every node whose value equals val and return the new head.
statement:
Remove every node whose value equals `val` from the list starting at `head`, and return the head of the resulting list.

The head itself may need to be removed, possibly several times in a row.

For example removing 7 from `[7,7,7,7]` leaves an empty list. A dummy node in front of the head lets you remove the head like any other node.
hints: Removing a node means changing the next pointer of the node before it. What about the head, which has no node before it?
Put a dummy node in front of head, so every real node has a predecessor.
Walk with a pointer to the previous node: if prev.next has the value, skip it (prev.next = prev.next.next); otherwise advance prev. Return dummy.next.
explain: Both nodes with value 6 are removed and the rest keep their order, leaving `[1,2,3,4,5]`.

title: Add Two Numbers
summary: Two non-negative numbers are stored as linked lists of digits in reverse order (ones digit first). Return their sum in the same form.
statement:
Two non-negative integers are stored as linked lists of digits in reverse order: the first node holds the ones digit. For example, `[2,4,3]` is 342.

Return the sum of the two numbers as a linked list in the same reverse order. Neither number has leading zeros except the number 0 itself.
hints: Reverse order is convenient: it is the order in which you add digits by hand, from the ones place up.
Walk both lists together with a carry. Each new digit is (a + b + carry) % 10 and the new carry is the sum / 10.
Keep going while either list has nodes left or the carry is non-zero, treating a missing digit as 0.
explain: The lists hold 342 and 465 with the ones digit first. 342 + 465 = 807, stored the same way as `[7,0,8]`.

title: Reverse Linked List II
summary: Reverse the nodes from position left to position right (1-indexed, inclusive) in one pass and return the head.
statement:
Reverse the part of the list from position `left` to position `right` (positions start at 1, both ends included) and return the head of the list.

Try to do it in one pass.

If `left` equals `right` the list is unchanged. A dummy node before the head handles `left = 1`, where the head itself moves.
hints: Find the node just before position left. A dummy head handles left = 1.
Reverse the next (right − left + 1) nodes the usual way, remembering the node where the reversed part starts (it becomes its tail).
Reconnect: the node before the section points to the new section head, and the old section head points to the node after the section. Or repeatedly move the next node to the front of the section.
explain: Positions 2 to 4 hold 2, 3, 4. Reversing only that part gives 4, 3, 2 while 1 and 5 stay in place: `[1,4,3,2,5]`.

title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
summary: Swap every two adjacent nodes (by relinking nodes, not by changing values) and return the head.
statement:
Swap every two adjacent nodes of the list and return its head: `1 → 2 → 3 → 4` becomes `2 → 1 → 4 → 3`. If the length is odd, the last node stays where it is.

Change the links between nodes; do not just swap their values.
hints: Each step works on a pair (a, b) and the node before it, prev. A dummy head gives the first pair a prev.
Rewire: prev.next = b, a.next = b.next, b.next = a. Then a is the prev of the next pair.
Stop when fewer than two nodes remain. Recursion also works: swap the first two and attach swapPairs(rest).
explain: Nodes are swapped two at a time: (1, 2) becomes 2, 1 and (3, 4) becomes 4, 3. The result is `[2,1,4,3]`.

title: Partition List
summary: Move every node with value less than x before the nodes with value ≥ x, keeping the original relative order within each part.
statement:
Rearrange the list so that every node with a value less than `x` comes before every node with a value greater than or equal to `x`.

Keep the original relative order of the nodes within each of the two groups, and return the head.
hints: Build two separate lists as you walk: one for values < x and one for the rest.
Use a dummy head and a tail pointer for each list, appending nodes in the order you meet them.
Join the "less" list's tail to the "rest" list's head, and set the end of the "rest" list to null so you do not create a cycle.
explain: Nodes smaller than 3 (1, 2, 2) come first, then the rest (4, 3, 5), each group keeping its original order: `[1,2,2,4,3,5]`.

title: Rotate List
summary: Rotate the list to the right by k places (k may exceed the length) and return the new head.
statement:
Rotate the list to the right by `k` places: each step moves the last node to the front. Return the new head.

`k` can be much larger than the length of the list.

Rotating by the list's length gives back the same list, so only `k mod length` steps matter. Join the tail to the head, then cut at the new end.
hints: Rotating by the list length gives the same list back, so only k % length matters.
Find the length and the tail in one pass, then connect the tail to the head to make a ring.
Walk length − (k % length) steps from the old tail; that node is the new tail. Its next is the new head; cut the ring there.
explain: Rotating right by 2 moves the last two nodes, 4 and 5, to the front: `[4,5,1,2,3]`.

title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
summary: Reverse the nodes k at a time; a final group shorter than k stays as it is. Use O(1) extra memory.
statement:
Reverse the nodes of the list `k` at a time and return the head. If the number of nodes left at the end is less than `k`, those nodes keep their order.

Change the links, not the values, and use only O(1) extra memory.
hints: Handle one group at a time: first check that k nodes remain, and stop if they do not.
Reverse exactly k nodes with the usual three-pointer loop, keeping a pointer to the node before the group (start with a dummy).
After reversing, the group's old first node is its new last node: connect it to the rest of the list and make it the "before" node of the next group.
explain: With `k = 2`, the groups (1, 2) and (3, 4) are reversed. The last group has only one node, fewer than `k`, so it stays as it is: `[2,1,4,3,5]`.
